classification_legend.invariant: Present in nearly all 46 reference reels (typically 40+/46). Treat as a hard rule — violate only with strong justification.
classification_legend.frequent: Present in a clear majority but not all reels (roughly 24-39/46). Treat as the default choice unless the scenario specifically calls for a variation.
classification_legend.optional: A recurring but non-majority choice (roughly 7-24/46). Legitimate to use, never required; pick when it serves the specific scenario.
classification_legend.one_off: Observed in only 1-3 reels. Not part of the reusable house style. Included here only for reference; do not treat as the default and do not build the generate-script pipeline around it.

format_outliers_do_not_replicate.name: Then vs Now relationship montage
format_outliers_do_not_replicate.why_it_is_an_outlier: Multi-location montage across 6+ distinct settings with almost no dialogue, resolving on a deadpan domestic punchline instead of the dominant single static two-shot scene. Also drives the rapid fast-cut editing one-off (10-18+ cuts, sub-1s average shot length).
format_outliers_do_not_replicate.instruction: Do not use as a template for generate-script. The house style is single-scene, low-cut, static-camera — this reel is the exception that proves it.

format_outliers_do_not_replicate.name: Paul monologue with live-action B-roll
format_outliers_do_not_replicate.why_it_is_an_outlier: Direct-to-camera mock-motivational-video parody ('message to all husbands') intercut with live-action product B-roll (watch, coffee, pen), punctured by a submissive reveal from an unseen off-screen character. Also drives the rapid fast-cut editing one-off.
format_outliers_do_not_replicate.instruction: Do not mix live-action footage into generated output and do not default to direct-to-camera monologue address. The house style is a two-character scene shot as if by an unseen third-person camera.

format_outliers_do_not_replicate.name: Fast-cut restaurant piece
format_outliers_do_not_replicate.why_it_is_an_outlier: Rapid-fire fast-cut editing (10-18+ cuts, sub-1-second average shot length) used for mock-commercial pacing instead of the dominant slow two-shot format.
format_outliers_do_not_replicate.instruction: Do not default to fast-cut montage pacing. The house editing style is 0-6 hard cuts total at 2-7s average shot length.

typical_beat_timing.total_runtime: Roughly 9.5-17.5 seconds as a single-scene micro-sketch (invariant, 45/46). This is well under the 20-25s range assumed elsewhere in the pipeline docs — new scripts should aim for this shorter runtime by default.
typical_beat_timing.cold_open: 0:00 — dialogue/action begins already in progress, mid-conversation or mid-argument, with zero establishing shot or context-setting narration (invariant, 43/46).
typical_beat_timing.hook_and_setup_fused: Roughly the first 30-45% of runtime — the hook (attention-grabbing opening line/situation) and the setup (context for the joke) are not staged as separate escalating beats; they are compressed into one continuous exchange (frequent, 36/46).
typical_beat_timing.minimal_conflict_beat: Mid-clip — there is no external obstacle or physical conflict. The 'conflict' is only a held silence or a single skeptical follow-up question, never an escalating argument (frequent, 34/46).
typical_beat_timing.build_up_pause: Immediately before the punchline (or immediately after it) — the single longest silence in the entire clip, roughly 0.6-3.3 seconds, longer than any other pause in the video (invariant, 43/46).
typical_beat_timing.punchline: Delivered as either a very short 1-3 word capitulation/verdict line ('No.', 'Good.', 'Yeah.') (frequent, 27/46) or as one unbroken escalating sentence with no internal pause, arriving right after the build-up pause (optional, 18/46).
typical_beat_timing.post_punchline_hold: 1-3 seconds of trailing silence follows the last line of dialogue before the cut to the outro card; no reaction shot or reply is required (frequent, 30/46 for the trailing silence; optional, 17/46 for withholding a reaction shot entirely).
typical_beat_timing.outro_card: Hard cut to a static black branded outro card with no narrative resolution, reply, or character button (invariant, 46/46). Frequently includes a yellow ticket/ribbon 'return tomorrow' CTA graphic (frequent, 39/46) and an 'Episode NN' + episode title label burned into the corner of the hook shot at the start (frequent, 30/46).

rules.rule: Keep total runtime to roughly 9.5-17.5 seconds as a single, unbroken scene. Do not write multi-scene scripts or pad runtime toward 20-25s.
Open in medias res: the scene must already be underway when the video starts. Never open on an establishing shot, narration, or scene-setting text.

Fuse the hook and setup into a single continuous exchange rather than writing them as two separate escalating beats. The audience should learn the premise and hit the first laugh-adjacent beat within the same breath of dialogue.
Do not write an external obstacle, physical conflict, or escalating argument. The only 'conflict' should be a held silence or a single skeptical follow-up question before the reveal.

End every script on a hard cut to a static black branded outro card. Never resolve the scene narratively, never show a reply to the punchline, never give a character a closing button line after the joke lands.
Default to including a 'return tomorrow' style CTA graphic on the outro card (in the reference reels, a yellow ticket/ribbon reading 'NEW EPISODE DAILY').
Default to burning an episode/scenario label into the corner of the opening shot (in the reference reels, 'Episode NN' plus a short episode title such as 'THAT LOOK').
Do not use a multi-location montage structure with near-zero dialogue as the default format.
Do not use a direct-to-camera monologue/parody structure intercut with other footage as the default format.

Write very little dialogue: 1-8 short lines total per script, averaging roughly 3-12 words per line. Resist the urge to over-explain the premise or the objection — the scenario should be legible from a handful of clipped lines.

Keep both characters' vocal delivery close in tone and register to one another — flat, similarly-paced, non-overlapping turns. (In the source reels this is evidenced indirectly: automated speaker diarization frequently collapsed a clear two-person exchange into a single speaker tag, implying the two voices read as tonally similar rather than sharply differentiated or interruptive.)

It is acceptable, and sometimes preferable for clarity, to write a cleanly alternating two-speaker back-and-forth (one line each, alternating) rather than folding both voices into one blended exchange.
Place the single longest silence in the whole script either immediately before or immediately after the punchline line — it should be measurably longer than any other pause in the piece.
Make the shortest line in the script (1-3 words: 'No.', 'Good.', 'Yeah.', or an equally clipped equivalent) do the work of the punchline or a capitulation/button line.

As an alternative to the ultra-short punchline, deliver the punchline as one unbroken sentence with no internal pause, using a front-loaded escalating clause structure, landing immediately after the script's biggest build-up pause.

dialogue.voice_notes: Dialogue in this style is written to be said, not read: short, clipped, declarative sentences with low pitch variation and no expressive vocal escalation, even when the content is emotionally loaded (see comedy/deadpan and audio/no-vocal-escalation rules). Lines should read like the character has already emotionally checked out of the stakes of the conversation — flat statements and flat questions, never raised-voice arguing, never trailing off with ellipses or interruptions. Avoid exclamation points in the script text; avoid stage directions implying vocal intensity ('shouts', 'exclaims'). The punchline in particular should be writable as a complete, grammatically plain sentence or a bare 1-3 word reply — nothing needs a vocal flourish to land because the pause around it (see structure.build_up_pause) is doing the comedic work, not the delivery.

rules.rule: Every line, including the punchline, should be playable deadpan: flat, matter-of-fact delivery regardless of how emotionally loaded the content is. Deadpan is the primary comedic engine of this style, not a garnish on top of a joke that is otherwise 'performed' — do not write jokes that depend on an animated or exaggerated reaction to land.

Treat the held pause as its own comedic beat, not just a gap between lines. Script an explicit awkward-silence moment (via a stage direction / pause marker) that itself performs part of the joke — the discomfort of the silence is the payoff, not filler waiting for the next line.

Structure the joke as irony/misdirection: open with a sincere- or serious-sounding claim or question, then undercut it with a mundane, petty, or absurd reveal. The gap between the register of the setup and the pettiness of the reveal is where the laugh comes from.

Root the joke's specificity in one hyper-concrete, quantified detail — an exact number, a specific day, a specific price, a specific product — rather than broad exaggeration or vague generalization. Recognition of the precise detail is the humor mechanism.

Do not write physical slapstick or a visual sight gag to carry the joke. Comedy should be dialogue- and micro-expression-driven within an otherwise static, locked-off frame — the humor lives in what is said and the flatness with which it's said, not in staged physical business.

It is acceptable to withhold any reaction shot or reply after the punchline and cut straight from the joke to the outro card with no capper — the audience does not need to see the other character's response for the joke to register as complete.

A physical sight gag as the payoff (rather than a spoken line) is a rare, non-default option — use only if a scenario specifically benefits from a single, contained sight gag (e.g., a small physical prop action), and keep it as understated as the rest of the style, never full slapstick.
rules.evidence: 2/46 reels — treat as a rare exception, not a technique to reach for by default

rules.rule: Cast exactly two on-screen principal characters carrying the entire scene. In the reference reels this pair is a heterosexual long-term couple (husband/wife); when adapting to a new niche, preserve the two-hander structure and the established, familiar-with-each-other relational dynamic between the pair.

Give both characters a shared 'low battery' resting facial design: permanently heavy-lidded/half-closed eyes and a flat, slightly downturned mouth as the default expression — and keep that resting expression in play regardless of what the dialogue content is (even when a line is emotionally charged, the face stays flat).
Give characters an elongated, exaggerated wedge/conical nose (especially the male character), often paired with small round glasses.
Have one character (commonly the male character) hold or fixate on a phone/device while the other speaks, visually enacting distraction or disengagement rather than active listening.

Avoid direct eye contact between the two characters even during the tensest beat of the exchange — have both face forward toward the camera/a shared focal point (e.g., a TV, in the sales-objection adaptation a shared screen) rather than turning to look at each other.
It is a strong option, though not required, to give the punchline or verdict line to the female character (in an adapted cast: the character in the 'reactive'/decision-holding role).

An unseen/off-screen second character who is spoken about or heard but never shown, delivering a twist purely through the on-screen character's reaction, is a rare available option — not the default two-hander, but usable if a scenario calls for a third implied party.

Never pan or tilt the camera. Every shot change must be a hard cut between fully static, locked-off setups — the camera itself should never be seen to move within a shot except for the one permitted push-in (see next rule).
It is a valid and clean option to play the entire joke in one unbroken static shot with zero internal cuts, rather than cutting between characters at all.

The only camera movement permitted anywhere in the piece is a slow, continuous, straight-line push-in (zoom toward a character's face) — never a pan, tilt, orbit, or handheld move — and it should be timed to land tight right on the punchline.
Default to a shot/reverse-shot pattern: open on a wide static two-shot establishing both characters and the setting, then cut to isolated close-ups on each speaker's face for their individual lines.

Hold a tight close-up on one character's face alone (with the partner cropped out of frame or softly blurred) specifically for the punchline delivery, isolating the deadpan reaction/delivery from the rest of the scene.

Symmetrical, centered, Wes-Anderson-style framing with a shallow-depth-of-field, softly blurred crowd of background extras is a strong option specifically for public/social settings (e.g., a restaurant or diner backdrop).

Render in 3D CGI with a felted-wool/clay-look shader designed to evoke stop-motion — but explicitly do NOT simulate genuine frame-by-frame stop-motion. There should be no set jitter, no visible fingerprints or tool marks in the material, and lighting/camera movement should stay perfectly smooth and consistent frame to frame (this is a stop-motion-styled CG look, not a stop-motion simulation).
Do not animate blinking. Characters' eyes stay open in the heavy-lidded default pose for the entire clip.

Concentrate essentially all animation budget on the face — mouth, eyebrows, eyelids. Keep the torso, arms, and legs locked and static with no idle secondary motion (no breathing sway, no cloth simulation, no hair simulation) for the majority of the shot.

Sync mouth movement to a small library of discrete, held/swapped viseme shapes timed to spoken words, rather than continuous, fluid phoneme-level lip sync — the mouth should read as changing between distinct held poses, not smoothly morphing.
Keep all background and set props (furniture, dishes, window light, wall decor) completely static across the shot — zero ambient motion, no wind, no flicker, no drift.

It is acceptable to give each character exactly one recurring physical gesture (e.g., a glasses-fidget, a phone-scroll, a knitting motion) that loops or holds for most of the shot, rather than continuously re-animating new business for the body.
Keep the total cut count low: 0-6 hard cuts for the entire piece. This is a slow, static-shot-driven format, not a fast-cut one.
Use hard cuts almost exclusively for every transition. Reserve dissolves/wipes, if used at all, only for the transition into the outro card.
Let a silent reaction/hold beat follow the punchline before cutting to the outro card, rather than cutting away from the joke immediately.
Aim for an average shot length of roughly 2-7 seconds across the piece.

Do not default to rapid-fire fast-cut montage editing (10-18+ cuts, sub-1-second average shot length). That pacing is a rare format outlier in the source set, used for a mock-commercial/montage piece, not the house style.
Include no background music anywhere in the piece.
Include no sound effects or foley of any kind.

Cluster pause duration around the punchline: make the single longest silence in the whole clip (roughly 0.6-3.3 seconds) land either as a build-up beat immediately before the punchline or as a trailing hold immediately after it.
Deliver dialogue as short, clipped, low-pitch-variation declarative sentences — not expressive or escalating vocal performance, even at emotionally loaded moments.
Let roughly 1-3 seconds of trailing silence follow the very last line of dialogue before the hard cut to the outro card.
Use a single unchanging set/location for the entire episode. Do not change location or scene — the only visual variety should come from reframing between wide and close shots of the same background.

Light the scene with warm, soft, naturalistic light from a single practical motivated source (e.g., a table lamp, a window, a candle — in an adapted context, a laptop/monitor glow works as the equivalent motivated source), with a shallow depth of field softly blurring the background.
Default to a domestic interior setting (kitchen, bedroom, or living-room couch equivalent) unless the scenario specifically calls for a public/social setting.
A public/social location (restaurant, park, sidewalk, parking garage, car, salon) is a legitimate alternative to a home interior when the scenario calls for it.
Include a smartphone or laptop as a visible on-screen prop tied directly to the scene's plot or joke — not just set dressing.
A visible wedding/engagement ring (or an equivalent small, legible prop that signals the characters' established relationship/role to each other) is an optional but effective detail.

veo3_style_keywords: MATERIAL: felted-wool / soft clay stop-motion-look shader on all characters and props — matte, fibrous, non-reflective surface, no glossy CG highlights

MATERIAL: CG-clean stop-motion pastiche — perfectly smooth motion, NO set jitter, NO visible fingerprints or tool marks, NO frame strobing; this is a stylized stop-motion LOOK rendered with fully consistent CG smoothness, not genuine frame-by-frame stop-motion
CHARACTER DESIGN: heavy-lidded, half-closed 'low battery' eyes as the default resting expression, no blinking during the shot
CHARACTER DESIGN: flat, slightly downturned mouth at rest, held even through emotionally loaded lines — deadpan face sculpt, not an expressive/animated face rig
CHARACTER DESIGN: elongated wedge/conical nose; small round glasses on at least one character

PROMPT-CRAFT NOTE (not a visual trait — supersedes any earlier, softer version of this rule): when reference images are attached, do not describe character appearance in the prompt text AT ALL, not even briefly by name/role — simply state that reference images are attached for each character and that they must be animated exactly as shown. Any appearance text in the prompt, however short, risks competing with and overriding image conditioning; real test generations drifted from the reference images until this was removed entirely
RIG/ANIMATION: animate only the mouth, eyebrows, and eyelids; keep torso, arms, and legs completely locked and static — no idle breathing sway, no cloth simulation, no hair simulation
RIG/ANIMATION: mouth reads as a small set of discrete held viseme poses swapped on each spoken word, not continuous fluid phoneme-level lip-sync
RIG/ANIMATION: at most one small looping gesture per character (e.g., tapping a keyboard, adjusting glasses, scrolling a phone) held for most of the shot rather than continuously re-animated

NICHE CREATIVE ADAPTATION (not reel-sourced — supersedes the older 'settled attentiveness' note, see the Style Bible's Niche Creative Adaptations section): characters actively, visibly react to each other's lines — human-scale, restrained expression, not exaggerated/anime — including a brief reactive glance toward one's own screen or the other participant's tile. This deliberately overrides the source reels' 'no reaction, no eye contact' default for this niche only
CAMERA: locked-off, static camera for every shot — no pans, no tilts, no handheld shake
CAMERA: the only allowed camera movement is a slow, continuous, straight-line push-in toward a character's face, timed to land tight exactly on the punchline line

CAMERA: shot/reverse-shot pattern — open on a wide static two-shot, cut to isolated tight close-ups per speaker, partner cropped out of frame or softly blurred during the other's line — this is a hard cut, not a zoom; a zoom-out/zoom-back-in choreography following the conversation appears in only 1 of 46 reference reels and is flagged there as the sole exception, not a pattern to build on

UI ADDITION (niche-specific, not reel-sourced): whichever character is currently speaking has a highlighted/glowing colored border ring around their Google Meet tile for the span they're talking; the other tile stays in its plain unhighlighted state; neither tile is highlighted during a shared silence. Reference images: references/layout/gmeet-active-speaker.png (highlighted) and references/layout/gmeet-normal.png (plain).
LIGHTING: warm, soft, naturalistic key light motivated by a single practical in-frame source (desk lamp, window, laptop/monitor glow); shallow depth of field with a softly blurred background
SET: completely static background — furniture, screens, props, and decor do not move, drift, flicker, or animate at all between frames
SET: single unchanging location for the whole scene; visual variety comes only from reframing between the wide two-shot and tight close-ups, never a location change
COLOR: muted, warm, desaturated palette consistent with a felt/clay material — avoid glossy or highly saturated CG rendering
COMPOSITION (optional, for public settings): symmetrical, centered Wes-Anderson-style framing with a shallow-DOF, softly blurred crowd of background extras
EDIT/PACING: 0-6 hard cuts total, no dissolves or wipes except optionally into the closing card; average shot length 2-7 seconds
AUDIO: no score, no sound design, no foley, no ambient room noise of any kind — complete silence except the spoken dialogue itself; do not add any environmental or 'authenticity' audio

PERFORMANCE: every line, including the punchline, delivered in a flat, low-pitch-variation, deadpan monotone regardless of emotional stakes (this describes the source reels; see the niche-adaptation override immediately below for how this niche should actually be prompted)

NICHE CREATIVE ADAPTATION (not reel-sourced): vocal delivery for this niche is naturalistic and restrained-awkward rather than strict flat monotone — a reluctant line should sound genuinely reluctant (soft, hesitant), not robotic; keep it low-key and human, never escalated or exaggerated
PERFORMANCE: hold a long silence (0.6-3.3s) directly before or after the punchline; no filler movement or sound during the hold
GRAPHIC OVERLAY (optional): burned-in episode/scenario label in the corner of the opening shot; static branded end-card with hard cut, no narrative resolution shown after it

NICHE CREATIVE ADAPTATION (not reel-sourced): an opening silent 'settling in' business beat (e.g. the Sales Rep writing something in a notebook) before any dialogue starts is now standard for this niche — gives editing room for a blurred topic-card overlay added afterward (same treatment as the outro card, not generated with Veo3) and doubles as a small character beat; keep it low-key and silent, no dialogue

NICHE CREATIVE ADAPTATION (not reel-sourced): the comedic core for this niche is awkwardness — pacing and expression — not a punchline mechanism; held silences and readable discomfort matter more than forcing a hyper-specific 'undercut' final line the way the source reels' punchlines do
prompt_generation_guidelines.script_structure_template:
TOTAL RUNTIME TARGET: 9.5-17.5s single unbroken scene (adapt: sales rep + prospect on a Google Meet call, two-person, established/familiar dynamic, in place of the reference reels' married couple).

[0:00] COLD OPEN — Cut in already mid-conversation. No establishing shot, no narration. Static locked-off wide two-shot (e.g., a split-screen / Meet-tile framing) showing both participants already engaged.

[~0:00-0:05] HOOK + SETUP (fused) — 1-3 short declarative lines (roughly 3-12 words each), deadpan delivery, low pitch variation. The objection (e.g., 'it's too expensive', 'I'll think about it') surfaces here, stated plainly rather than argued. Optional: one participant fixates on a phone/second screen/laptop rather than making direct eye contact with the camera/other tile.

[~0:05-0:08] MINIMAL CONFLICT BEAT — No escalating argument. Either a held silence or exactly one skeptical follow-up question/pushback line.

[~0:08-0:10] BUILD-UP PAUSE — The single longest silence in the script, 0.6-3.3s, placed immediately before the punchline. Optional: this is where the sole camera push-in (slow, straight-line, toward one character's face) lands.

[~0:10-0:12] PUNCHLINE — Either a 1-3 word capitulation/verdict line, or one unbroken escalating sentence delivered with no internal pause. Structure it as irony/misdirection (a sincere-sounding claim undercut by a mundane, petty, or absurd reveal) or as recognition humor anchored on one hyper-specific quantified detail (an exact price, day, or number). Cut to a tight close-up on the speaker's face alone, deadpan, partner cropped/blurred out.

[~0:12-0:14] POST-PUNCHLINE HOLD — 1-3s of trailing silence. No reaction shot or reply is required; camera holds static.

[~0:14] HARD CUT TO OUTRO CARD — Static black branded end card (brand name + credit line). Optional: 'new content daily'-style CTA graphic and an episode/scenario label. No narrative resolution shown.

DO NOT: pad to 20-25s, add a second scene or location change, write an escalating argument, add music/SFX, use camera pans/tilts, use fast-cut montage editing, or resolve the objection with a visible reply/reaction after the punchline — these all break invariant or near-invariant rules of the house style.
